Narrative rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear beginning that sets up the moment, events in order with temporal words, details/dialogue showing feelings, ending that reflects on the lesson, few errors; 3 (proficient) = all parts present, some details, mostly correct capitals and punctuation; 2 = events listed with few details or no real ending; 1 = unclear or incomplete.

weeks.prep: Library books on California natural wonders (Yosemite, redwoods, Death Valley, Monterey Bay), a kid-safe search engine (e.g., Kiddle) or National Park Service pages, a dictionary.
misconceptions: Asking questions that are too broad ('Tell me about Yosemite') — narrow them ('How did glaciers shape Yosemite Valley?').
Using an index like a table of contents — the index is alphabetical at the back and lists exact pages.

days.guide: Show photos of the four wonders and let the child choose. Model one specific question, then the child writes 5 research questions.

questions.q: Give a strong research question about Death Valley.
questions.a: Why is Death Valley so hot and dry?

days.guide: Model choosing keywords (not whole sentences) and using a book's index. The child finds 3–4 sources and records title, author or website, and date on a source list.

questions.q: What keywords would you search to learn how tall redwoods grow?
questions.a: redwood height tallest tree.

days.guide: The child uses a dictionary and a book glossary to define 6 domain words (granite, glacier, canyon, habitat, erosion, kelp). Then spell inter- and trans- words.

questions.q: What does 'transport' mean?
questions.a: To carry from one place to another (trans = across).

questions.q: What is a glacier?
questions.a: A huge, slow-moving mass of ice.

days.guide: The child reads 2 sources and highlights or flags answers to the research questions, noting which questions still need answers. Model flagging one answer and writing the question number next to it.

questions.q: What is the tallest kind of tree on Earth, and where does it grow?
questions.a: The coast redwood, which grows along the northern California coast (and southern Oregon).

days.guide: Review the question list and source list together and give feedback. Give one compliment and one suggestion for narrowing or adding a question.

questions.q: What information belongs on a source list?
questions.a: The title, the author or website name, and the date.

weeks.assessment_key: Proficient: 5 specific, open-ended questions about the chosen wonder; at least 2 appropriate, reliable sources (library book, National Park Service, encyclopedia) listed with title and author or website.

weeks.prep: Note cards, the sources from last week, a two-column comparison chart.
misconceptions: Copying sentences word for word — notes must be short and in your own words, with the source written on each card.
Ignoring when sources disagree — check a third reliable source.

days.guide: Model reading a paragraph, covering it, and writing a short note from memory. The child takes notes on cards from source 1, one fact per card, labeled with the source.

questions.q: Write a note for: 'Half Dome is a granite dome that rises about 4,700 feet above the floor of Yosemite Valley.'
questions.a: Example: Half Dome — granite, about 4,700 ft above valley floor.

days.guide: The child sorts all cards into 4 piles: location, plants and animals, history, and visiting. Cards that don't fit go into an 'extra' pile.

questions.q: Name the 4 categories for sorting notes.
questions.a: Location, plants and animals, history, visiting.

days.guide: The child takes notes from source 2 and fills a chart showing key points each source gives on the same topics. Model one row of the chart, then let the child complete the rest.

questions.q: Why compare two sources?
questions.a: To check that facts agree and to find information one source left out.

days.guide: Find 4 unfamiliar words in the sources. Model using context clues (nearby words, examples) and affixes (un-, re-, -less) to figure out meanings, then check in a dictionary.

questions.q: What does 'endangered' mean in 'The California condor is an endangered bird'?
questions.a: In danger of dying out completely.

days.guide: The child writes a paragraph explaining what the two sources agree on and where they differ or give different information. Model the frame: 'Both sources say ___, but source 1 says ___ while source 2 says ___.'

questions.q: What should you do if two sources disagree on a fact?
questions.a: Check a third reliable source (such as a National Park Service site).

weeks.assessment_key: Proficient: 10+ notes in own words, each labeled with its source, sorted into the 4 categories; comparison paragraph names both sources and gives at least one point of agreement and one difference.

weeks.prep: Sorted notes, a map of California, a research rubric (intro, organized body paragraphs, facts in own words, conclusion, map with caption, source list).
misconceptions: Mixing categories within a paragraph — each paragraph covers one category.
Adding a map with no caption — the caption tells the reader what the map shows.

days.guide: Turn the sorted piles into an outline: introduction, one body paragraph per category, conclusion. Model ordering the cards within each pile so the paragraph flows logically.

questions.q: How many body paragraphs should the report have?
questions.a: One for each category — usually 3 or 4.

days.guide: Model a hook and topic sentence. The child drafts the introduction and two body paragraphs from the outline.

questions.q: What goes in an introduction?
questions.a: A hook that grabs the reader and a sentence stating the topic of the report.

days.guide: The child drafts the remaining body paragraph(s) and the conclusion, then draws or prints a map showing the location with a caption. Check that the conclusion restates the main idea and does not add brand-new facts.

questions.q: What should the map caption say?
questions.a: What the map shows, e.g., 'Yosemite National Park is in the Sierra Nevada mountains of eastern California.'

days.guide: Find words in the report with prefixes and suffixes and determine their meanings. Then review homographs (same spelling, different meanings).

questions.q: What does 'unprotected' mean? 'Rebuild'?
questions.a: Not protected; build again.

questions.q: Give a homograph and two meanings.
questions.a: Bat — a flying animal or a stick used in baseball (also: wind, bark, park).

days.guide: The child checks the draft against each line of the rubric and marks what still needs work. Have the child highlight evidence for each rubric line in the draft.

questions.q: Name one item on the research rubric.
questions.a: Example: facts written in my own words.

weeks.assessment_key: Draft proficient: introduction, organized body paragraphs (one category each), conclusion, captioned map; rubric self-check completed honestly with at least one revision goal.

weeks.prep: Computer or tablet, poster board or slideshow software, a printer for a photo and map. Write the Unit 8 test with a new informational passage.
misconceptions: Putting too many words on slides or posters — use headings, pictures and a few key facts.
Reading the poster aloud instead of talking — the speaker explains; the visual supports.

days.guide: Read the draft together. First check facts and organization, then spelling, capitals and punctuation, with the child making the changes.

questions.q: What should you check first when revising?
questions.a: Facts and organization, then spelling and punctuation.

days.guide: The child types the final report and adds a photo and the captioned map, crediting the photo source. Have the child proofread the typed copy aloud to catch typing errors.

questions.q: Why should you credit where a photo came from?
questions.a: It is someone else's work, and readers can see the source.

days.guide: The child makes a poster or 4–6 slides with a title, headings, pictures and key facts. Remind them that each slide or section should match one report paragraph.

questions.q: What belongs on a presentation visual?
questions.a: A title, headings, pictures and a few key facts — not whole paragraphs.

days.guide: The child presents to the family using the visuals and answers questions. Have each family member ask one question, and praise answers that use report facts.

questions.q: What should you say if you don't know the answer to a question?
questions.a: 'I don't know, but I can find out,' and then look it up.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test and score the report and presentation with the rubric. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: What does a glossary do?
questions.a: Gives the definitions of important words in a text.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test (new passage): 1) Main idea 2) Two key details 3) Purpose of one text feature 4) Context-clue meaning of a word 5) Meaning of a prefixed word 6) Compare with a second short text: one similarity 7) one difference 8) Name a reliable source type. Proficient 6+/8. Report rubric: 4 = accurate facts in the child's own words, organized into paragraphs with topic sentences, an introduction and conclusion, text features or visuals, few errors; 3 (proficient) = organized and accurate with minor gaps; 2 = facts listed with weak organization or copied wording; 1 = incomplete. Presentation: clear voice, eye contact, visuals used.

weeks.prep: The Tale of Peter Rabbit and The Tale of Benjamin Bunny by Beatrix Potter (Project Gutenberg editions include her illustrations).
misconceptions: Thinking Peter Rabbit is only a funny story — it shows the consequences of disobeying.
Confusing plot (what happens) with theme (the message).

days.guide: Read The Tale of Peter Rabbit aloud, enjoying the pictures. The child maps the plot: beginning, problem, events, climax, resolution.

questions.q: What did Peter's mother warn him about?
questions.a: Not to go into Mr. McGregor's garden, because his father had an accident there and was put in a pie by Mrs. McGregor.

questions.q: How does Peter escape?
questions.a: He hides in a watering can, then finds the gate and squeezes under it; Mr. McGregor later uses Peter's lost jacket and shoes for a scarecrow.

days.guide: Read The Tale of Benjamin Bunny and map its plot the same way. Ask the child what is the same and what is new compared to the first tale.

questions.q: Why do Peter and Benjamin go back to the garden?
questions.a: To get Peter's clothes back from the scarecrow.

questions.q: Who rescues them from the cat?
questions.a: Old Mr. Benjamin Bunny, Benjamin's father.

days.guide: Fill a chart comparing setting, characters, problem, solution and theme of the two tales. Show how a dictionary shows syllables (gar·den) and practice reading them.

questions.q: What setting do the two tales share?
questions.a: Mr. McGregor's garden.

questions.q: How is Peter's mood different in the second tale?
questions.a: He is nervous and scared, while Benjamin is bold and confident.

days.guide: The child writes a comparison paragraph with at least 2 similarities and 2 differences. Provide a frame: 'Both tales ___. However, in the first tale ___, while in the second ___.'

questions.q: What theme do both tales share?
questions.a: Disobeying and going where you shouldn't can lead to trouble.

days.guide: Ask the comparison questions in the key; the child reads a Potter passage aloud fluently. Time a one-minute read and note phrasing and expression.

questions.q: What did Peter's mother give him when he got home sick?
questions.a: Chamomile tea.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison questions: 1) Shared setting → Mr. McGregor's garden 2) Shared character → Peter 3) Who gets Peter out of trouble in each? → he escapes alone in the first; Old Mr. Benjamin Bunny in the second 4) Shared theme → disobeying leads to trouble. Paragraph rubric: 4 = 2 similarities and 2 differences with details; 3 = 1 each; 2 = summary only; 1 = inaccurate. Fluency: 3 = smooth and expressive; 2 = some hesitations; 1 = word-by-word.

weeks.prep: A short readers' theater script adapted from a fable or Potter tale (search 'readers theater Aesop' for free scripts), highlighters, a recording device.
misconceptions: Reading stage directions aloud — they tell actors what to do and are not spoken.
Rushing lines — slow down, pause, and use expression.

days.guide: Read a sample script together. The child highlights the cast list, scene headings and stage directions and explains each one's purpose.

questions.q: What are stage directions?
questions.a: Instructions in brackets or italics that tell actors what to do; they are not read aloud.

days.guide: Model turning one narration line into dialogue. The child converts a fable into a short script with a narrator, characters and 2–3 scenes.

questions.q: Turn 'The fox asked the crow to sing' into a script line.
questions.a: FOX: Oh, beautiful Crow, won't you sing a song for me?

days.guide: Rehearse the script several times. Coach volume, expression and waiting for cues.

questions.q: How should the narrator read?
questions.a: Clearly and steadily, setting the scene for the audience.

days.guide: Perform the script for the family and record it. Remind performers to face the audience and hold scripts below their faces.

questions.q: Why record a performance?
questions.a: To watch it later and see what went well and what to improve.

days.guide: Watch the recording together. The child reflects on what went well and explains how each scene built on the one before.

questions.q: How do scenes build on each other in a play?
questions.a: Each scene moves the plot forward — introducing the problem, building to the turning point, then the ending.

weeks.assessment_key: Script: 3 = cast list, 2+ scenes, dialogue for each character, stage directions; 2 = missing one element; 1 = incomplete. Performance: 3 = expressive, clear and on cue; 2 = mostly clear; 1 = hard to follow.

weeks.prep: Writing folder, reading log, a folder for the portfolio. Write the end-of-year assessment (short passage plus spelling and grammar items).
misconceptions: Choosing favorite pieces instead of best work — pick pieces that show your strongest skills.
Writing general reflections ('I got better') — give specific examples.

days.guide: Look through the reading log together. The child chooses a top 3 and writes a recommendation for one.

questions.q: What makes a good book recommendation?
questions.a: The title and author, a short summary without spoiling the ending, and reasons someone would enjoy it.

days.guide: The child chooses their best narrative, informative and opinion pieces and writes a note for each explaining why it was chosen. Have the child explain what skill each piece shows best.

questions.q: Why include all three types of writing?
questions.a: Each shows different skills: telling a story, teaching facts and supporting an opinion.

days.guide: Give the end-of-year assessment. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: What is the past tense of 'bring'?
questions.a: brought.

days.guide: The child writes a letter to their future 4th-grade self about growth, favorite books and goals. Encourage specific examples, like a book that was hard at first or a piece of writing they're proud of.

questions.q: What should the letter include?
questions.a: Specific ways they grew as a reader and writer, favorite books, and goals for next year.

days.guide: Hold a family reading celebration where the child shares the portfolio and sets a summer reading goal. Let the child lead the sharing and celebrate effort as well as results.

questions.q: Give an example of a good summer reading goal.
questions.a: Read 10 chapter books by August and keep a reading log.

weeks.assessment_key: End-of-year assessment: Reading (short fable or passage): main idea or moral, character trait with evidence, theme. Spelling (10): unhappy, reread, hopeful, careless, quickly, kindness, cries, hopping, hoping, famous. Grammar: 1) plural of child → children 2) past of write → wrote 3) the toys of the boys → the boys' toys 4) punctuate dialogue: "Come here," said Mom. 5) combine with but 6) capitalize a title. Proficient: 80% overall. Portfolio: proficient with all three writing types and a specific reflection.

MATH.overview: Teach each lesson in three moves: model with objects or drawings, work a few problems together, then let the child practice independently while you watch for the week's listed misconceptions. From Week 11 on, keep a 5–10 minute daily fact-practice routine. Fridays are review and check: score the check with the answer key, reteach mistakes the following Monday, and don't move on from a concept the child cannot model with objects or drawings.

weeks.prep: Gather base-ten blocks (or paper flats/rods/units), a place value chart, 3 dice and digit cards 0-9. Write the 12 quiz items in the answer key on a sheet before Friday.
misconceptions: Reading 305 as 'thirty-five' or writing 3005 for three hundred five — use a place value chart and point out that the 0 holds the tens place empty.
Comparing by the last digit (thinking 298 > 301 because 8 > 1) — always compare hundreds first, then tens, then ones.

days.guide: Roll 3 dice, build the number with blocks (flats = hundreds, rods = tens, units = ones), then say it aloud. Model one: 'I rolled 4, 2, 6 — 426 is 4 flats, 2 rods, 6 units = 400 + 20 + 6.' The child builds and records 6 numbers in all three forms; check each block model matches the digits.

questions.q: Write 538 in expanded form and word form.
questions.a: 500 + 30 + 8; five hundred thirty-eight.

questions.q: What number is 7 hundreds, 0 tens, 4 ones?
questions.a: 704 (the zero shows there are no tens).

days.guide: Draw a long line labeled 0 and 1,000 and mark 500 first, then the other hundreds as benchmarks. Model placing 750 halfway between 700 and 800; the child places 10 numbers and tells which benchmark helped. Check that numbers are in order and roughly spaced correctly.

questions.q: Between which two hundreds is 462, and is it closer to 400 or 500?
questions.a: Between 400 and 500; closer to 500 because 462 is past the halfway point, 450.

questions.q: Where does 250 go on a 0–1,000 line?
questions.a: Halfway between 200 and 300.

days.guide: Model comparing by lining numbers up in a place value chart and checking hundreds, then tens, then ones. Remind the child the open side of < or > faces the greater number. The child compares 10 pairs and orders 6 numbers, saying which place decided each comparison.

questions.q: Compare 647 and 674 with <, > or =.
questions.a: 647 < 674 — the hundreds are equal, and 4 tens is less than 7 tens.

questions.q: Order from least to greatest: 509, 590, 95, 950.

days.guide: Play 'Greatest Number': each player draws 3 digit cards and arranges them to make the largest number; the greater number wins. Then show that 10 more/less changes the tens digit and 100 more/less changes the hundreds digit, using blocks for 395 → 405. The child writes 5 numbers with all four related numbers.

questions.q: With the digits 3, 8, 1, what are the greatest and least 3-digit numbers?
questions.a: Greatest 831; least 138.

questions.q: What is 10 more than 495? 100 less than 312?
questions.a: 505 (9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens, so the hundreds go up); 212.

days.guide: Give the 12-item quiz in the answer key without help. Afterward, rebuild any missed item with blocks and have the child explain the fix aloud.

questions.q: What is the value of the 6 in 862?
questions.a: 6 tens, or 60.

weeks.assessment_key: 1) 472 in expanded form → 400 + 70 + 2. 2) 305 in words → three hundred five. 3) 600 + 40 + 8 → 648. 4) six hundred nineteen → 619. 5) 527 __ 572 → <. 6) 890 __ 809 → >. 7) 400 + 30 + 6 __ 436 → =. 8) 10 more than 395 → 405. 9) 10 less than 702 → 692. 10) 100 more than 846 → 946. 11) 100 less than 1,000 → 900. 12) Order 318, 381, 183, 813 → 183, 318, 381, 813. Proficient: 10+/12 and block models match digits.

weeks.prep: Make number line strips (0–100 by tens; 0–1,000 by hundreds) and copy a grocery flyer or receipt. Write the 10-problem check from the answer key.
misconceptions: Rounding 450 down to 400 or 35 down to 30 — a number exactly halfway rounds up by convention.
Changing the wrong digit (rounding 347 to the nearest hundred as 350) — circle the place you are rounding to and look only at the digit just to its right.
Forgetting to regroup when rounding up from 9 (995 → 1,000; 96 → 100) — show it on the number line.

days.guide: Draw a vertical number line with the two tens around the number (e.g., 40 at the bottom, 50 at the top, 45 marked halfway). Ask 'Is 47 above or below the halfway mark?' so the child sees it rounds up to 50. The child rounds 15 numbers, marking each on a line first.

questions.q: Round 63 and 285 to the nearest ten.
questions.a: 63 → 60 (3 ones is less than 5); 285 → 290 (exactly halfway rounds up).

questions.q: Which two tens is 718 between, and what does it round to?
questions.a: 710 and 720; it rounds to 720.

days.guide: Repeat yesterday's routine on a 0–1,000 line, marking the halfway point (e.g., 350 between 300 and 400). The child rounds 15 numbers to the nearest hundred, saying the halfway number aloud each time. Check that they look at the tens digit to decide.

questions.q: Round 432 and 678 to the nearest hundred.
What is the halfway point between 800 and 900?

days.guide: Work through 450, 995 and 305 together on number lines. The child writes a sentence explaining why 450 rounds to 500 (it is exactly halfway and the rule is to round up). Have them invent two other tricky numbers and round them.

questions.q: Round 995 to the nearest ten and to the nearest hundred.
questions.a: Nearest ten: 1,000. Nearest hundred: 1,000.

questions.q: Round 305 to the nearest hundred and to the nearest ten.
questions.a: Nearest hundred: 300 (0 tens). Nearest ten: 310 (5 ones rounds up).

days.guide: Show a flyer price like $3.47 and ask which dimes and dollars it is between. The child rounds 6 prices to the nearest 10 cents and nearest dollar, then adds the rounded dollars to estimate a total. Compare the estimate to the exact total.

questions.q: Round $2.68 to the nearest dollar and the nearest 10 cents.
Estimate $1.89 + $4.12 + $2.95 to the nearest dollar.

days.guide: Give the 10-problem check, then have the child write a rounding rule in their own words. A good rule mentions finding the two benchmarks, checking the digit to the right (or the halfway point), and rounding up at 5 or more.

questions.q: In your own words, how do you round to the nearest hundred?
questions.a: Find the two hundreds the number is between and look at the tens digit — 0–4 rounds down to the lower hundred, 5–9 rounds up to the higher hundred.

weeks.assessment_key: Nearest 10: 1) 47 → 50 2) 82 → 80 3) 355 → 360 4) 921 → 920 5) 996 → 1,000. Nearest 100: 6) 238 → 200 7) 650 → 700 8) 449 → 400 9) 871 → 900 10) 52 → 100. Rule rubric: 3 = mentions benchmarks, the digit to the right, and the halfway/5 rule; 2 = rule correct but misses the halfway case; 1 = incomplete or incorrect.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks and a place value mat; write 8 word problems for Thursday (store, library, miles) and the quiz in the answer key.
misconceptions: Forgetting the regrouped 1 (367 + 248 = 505 instead of 615) — model trading 10 units for a rod with blocks and write the small 1 above the tens.
Adding digits without lining up places (405 + 37 with 37 under 40) — use grid paper or a place value chart so ones sit under ones.

days.guide: Model 367 + 248 on an open number line: start at 367, jump +200 to 567, +40 to 607, +8 to 615. The child solves 8 sums, drawing each jump. Check that the jumps add up to the second addend.

questions.q: Solve 256 + 138 on an open number line.

days.guide: Show partial sums: for 475 + 368 write 400 + 300 = 700, 70 + 60 = 130, 5 + 8 = 13, then 700 + 130 + 13 = 843. The child solves 8 problems this way, saying the value of each part (seventy, not seven).

questions.q: Use partial sums for 529 + 283.
Why do we write 70 + 60 and not 7 + 6?
questions.a: Because those digits are in the tens place, so they are worth 70 and 60.

days.guide: Build 158 + 276 with blocks: combine units (14, trade 10 for a rod), combine rods (13, trade 10 for a flat), combine flats. Record each trade in the standard algorithm as it happens. The child does 10 problems, using blocks for the first 3.

questions.q: Solve 158 + 276 with the standard algorithm.

days.guide: Before solving, round each addend to estimate. The child solves 8 word problems and writes 'reasonable' or 'check again' by comparing to the estimate.

questions.q: A library has 386 fiction and 427 nonfiction books. Estimate, then find the total.
questions.a: Estimate 400 + 400 = 800; exact 813 — reasonable.

questions.q: Sam says 312 + 289 = 501. Is that reasonable?
questions.a: No. 300 + 300 = 600, so 501 is too low; the correct sum is 601.

days.guide: Give the quiz; the child may use any strategy. Then have them explain one problem aloud, naming the strategy and each step.

questions.q: Explain how you could solve 495 + 305 mentally.
questions.a: 495 + 5 = 500, then 500 + 300 = 800 (move 5 over to make a friendly number).

weeks.assessment_key: 1) 243 + 152 = 395 2) 367 + 248 = 615 3) 158 + 276 = 434 4) 509 + 391 = 900 5) 625 + 185 = 810 6) 444 + 389 = 833 7) 299 + 450 = 749 8) 275 students Monday and 318 Tuesday → 593 students. Oral explanation: 3 = names strategy and explains place value in each step; 2 = correct steps, vague on place value; 1 = cannot explain. Proficient: 7+/8.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks, open number line paper, an addition table (0–10) for Thursday. Write the quiz in the answer key.
misconceptions: Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column (52 − 38 = 26) — model with blocks that you cannot take 8 units from 2 without trading a ten.
Errors across zeros (603 − 278) — show trading a flat for 10 rods, then a rod for 10 units: 603 becomes 5 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones.

days.guide: Model 603 − 278 by counting up: 278 + 2 = 280, + 20 = 300, + 300 = 600, + 3 = 603; the jumps total 2 + 20 + 300 + 3 = 325. The child solves 8 problems this way, adding the jumps carefully.

questions.q: Find 603 − 278 by counting up.
Find 500 − 347 by counting up.

days.guide: Show that adding the same amount to both numbers keeps the difference the same: 502 − 199 = 503 − 200 = 303. The child solves 10 problems by making the number being subtracted friendly, then checks one with blocks.

questions.q: Use compensation for 502 − 199.
Use compensation for 341 − 98.

days.guide: Build 425 with blocks and subtract 168: trade a rod for 10 units, then a flat for 10 rods, recording each trade in the algorithm. Practice across zeros with 700 − 254. The child does 10 problems.

questions.a: 446 (700 is regrouped as 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones).

days.guide: The child solves 8 subtraction problems and checks each by adding the answer to the number subtracted. Then look at an addition table together and notice that each row and column goes up by 1 and the table is symmetric.

questions.q: Solve 812 − 457 and check with addition.
What pattern do you see in the doubles 1 + 1, 2 + 2, 3 + 3 … on the addition table?
questions.a: The sums 2, 4, 6, 8 … are all even and go up by 2.

days.guide: Give the quiz. For each problem, ask which strategy is most efficient (counting up when numbers are close, compensation near a hundred, the algorithm otherwise).

questions.q: Which strategy fits 401 − 398 best, and why?
questions.a: Counting up — the numbers are close: 398 + 3 = 401, so the answer is 3.

weeks.prep: Bar model templates; a family trip mileage chart (e.g., Home→Zoo 128 mi, Zoo→Beach 245 mi, Beach→Home 310 mi). Write the Unit 1 test in the answer key.
misconceptions: Using a 'key word' rule (always adding for 'in all') — draw the bar model and decide which piece is unknown instead.
In start-unknown problems, adding when they should subtract — write the equation with a letter (n + 125 = 400) and use the inverse operation.

days.guide: Model a bar model: a long bar for the whole and smaller pieces for the parts, with '?' on the unknown. Do one each of result unknown, change unknown and start unknown. The child draws bars for 6 problems and solves.

questions.q: Ana had some stickers. She got 125 more and now has 400. How many did she start with?
A store had 512 apples and sold 238. How many are left?

days.guide: Turn each bar model into an equation with a letter for the unknown, such as 425 + n = 700. Solve using the inverse operation and substitute back to check.

questions.q: Solve 425 + n = 700.
Solve m − 160 = 340.

days.guide: Estimate first by rounding, then solve the two steps in order, labeling Step 1 and Step 2. The child solves 5 book-drive problems and compares to the estimates.

questions.q: The drive collected 214 books Monday and 189 Tuesday, then gave 250 to a school. How many are left?
questions.a: 214 + 189 = 403; 403 − 250 = 153 books. Estimate 200 + 200 − 250 = 150, so it is reasonable.

questions.q: They want 600 books and have 403. How many more do they need?

days.guide: Using the mileage chart, the child writes two original problems (one one-step, one two-step) and solves them; you solve them too and compare. Check that each problem has enough information and that the child's answers match yours.

questions.q: Home→Zoo is 128 mi and Zoo→Beach is 245 mi. How far from Home to the Beach through the Zoo?
questions.a: 373 miles.

questions.q: Beach→Home is 310 mi. How much longer is that than Zoo→Beach (245 mi)?
questions.a: 65 miles.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test without help. Review errors the next day with blocks or bar models.

questions.q: Round 649 to the nearest hundred and to the nearest ten.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test: 1) Round 76 to the nearest 10 → 80 2) Round 845 to the nearest 100 → 800 3) Round 350 to the nearest 100 → 400 4) 456 + 278 = 734 5) 390 + 415 = 805 6) 702 − 348 = 354 7) 600 − 199 = 401 8) 300 + n = 825 → n = 525 9) A farm had 438 hens, bought 126 more, then sold 200 → 364 10) Estimate 489 + 312 to the nearest hundred → 500 + 300 = 800. Proficient: 8+/10.

weeks.prep: Counters (beans or cereal), cups and paper plates, a hundreds chart, and real items or photos with equal groups (egg carton, window panes).
misconceptions: Confusing the number of groups with the number in each group — always say '3 groups of 7' while pointing to the plates, then the counters.
Thinking any groups count — multiplication needs equal groups; show plates with unequal amounts and ask whether 3 × 4 describes them.

days.guide: Put out 4 plates with 3 counters each and say '4 groups of 3 is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12, and we write 4 × 3 = 12.' The child makes 6 arrangements and writes both the repeated addition and the multiplication sentence.

questions.q: Write repeated addition and multiplication for 5 plates with 2 counters each.
What does 3 × 6 mean?
questions.a: 3 groups of 6, which is 18.

days.guide: Look at photos or objects with equal groups and ask 'How many groups? How many in each?' The child writes a multiplication equation for each picture.

questions.q: An egg carton has 2 rows of 6 eggs. Write an equation.
A window has 4 rows of 3 panes. How many panes?

days.guide: Skip count by 2s, 5s and 10s on a hundreds chart, coloring the numbers you land on. Show that the 6th number landed on when counting by 5s is 6 × 5 = 30.

questions.q: Skip count by 5s to find 7 × 5.
What is 8 × 10?

days.guide: Read each story and ask 'What are the groups and what is in each one?', then draw circles with dots. The child solves 6 problems and writes an equation for each.

questions.q: 4 bags have 6 apples each. How many apples?
questions.a: 4 × 6 = 24 apples.

questions.q: There are 5 cars with 4 wheels each. How many wheels?
questions.a: 5 × 4 = 20 wheels.

days.guide: Give the 10-picture matching check. Then the child writes and draws a story for 3 × 7.

questions.q: Write a story for 3 × 7.
questions.a: Example: 3 boxes each hold 7 crayons, so there are 21 crayons. (It must show 3 equal groups of 7 and the answer 21.)

weeks.assessment_key: Draw these 10 pictures and match: 2 groups of 5 → 2 × 5 = 10; 3 of 4 → 3 × 4 = 12; 4 of 2 → 8; 5 of 5 → 25; 6 of 3 → 18; 2 of 9 → 18; 4 of 4 → 16; 3 of 10 → 30; 7 of 2 → 14; 1 of 8 → 8. Proficient: 9/10 matched, and the 3 × 7 story shows 3 equal groups of 7 = 21.

weeks.prep: Square tiles (or paper squares), grid paper, a muffin tin and an egg carton for the array hunt. Write the quiz in the answer key.
misconceptions: Mixing up rows and columns — rows go across (like rows of seats), columns go up and down; label them on the first array.
Thinking 3 × 6 and 6 × 3 give different answers — rotate the same tile array to show the total stays 18.

days.guide: Build a 3 × 5 array of tiles and say '3 rows, 5 in each row, 3 × 5 = 15.' The child builds 10 arrays and labels rows × columns.

questions.q: Draw an array for 4 × 6. How many in all?
questions.a: 4 rows of 6 dots = 24.

questions.q: An array has 2 rows of 8. Write the equation.

days.guide: Draw a 3 × 6 array on paper, then turn the paper a quarter turn — now it is 6 rows of 3 and still 18. Introduce the word 'commutative.' The child records 8 turnaround pairs.

questions.q: If 7 × 4 = 28, what is 4 × 7?
questions.a: 28 — the commutative property says changing the order of factors does not change the product.

questions.q: Write the turnaround fact for 9 × 2 = 18.

days.guide: Hunt the house for arrays (muffin tin, egg carton, ice cube tray, buttons on a remote). For each one, write both equations.

questions.q: A muffin tin has 3 rows of 4 cups. Write two equations.
An ice cube tray has 2 rows of 7. How many cubes?

days.guide: Draw array problems on grid paper by shading rows. The child solves problems about chairs in rows and garden beds.

questions.q: Chairs are in 5 rows with 6 chairs each. How many chairs?
questions.a: 5 × 6 = 30 chairs.

questions.q: A garden has 4 rows of 9 carrots. How many carrots?

days.guide: Give the arrays quiz, then the child draws one array and explains the commutative property in writing. Check that the drawing shows the same array turned, not two different arrays.

questions.q: Explain why 2 × 5 = 5 × 2 with a drawing.
questions.a: An array of 2 rows of 5, turned sideways, is 5 rows of 2; it is the same 10 dots, so the products are equal.

weeks.assessment_key: 1) 3 × 4 = 12 2) 2 × 7 = 14 3) 5 × 5 = 25 4) 4 × 8 = 32 5) If 6 × 3 = 18, then 3 × 6 = 18 6) Draw 2 × 9 (2 rows of 9) = 18 7) 6 rows of 4 seats = 24 8) 3 rows of 10 = 30. Explanation: 3 = drawing shows the rotation and states order doesn't change the product; 2 = correct but no drawing or vague; 1 = incorrect. Proficient: 7+/8 and a 3 on the explanation.

weeks.prep: 24 counters, 8 cups, grapes or crackers (20+) and small bags, number line paper. Write the quiz in the answer key.
misconceptions: Thinking division only means 'sharing' — show the other meaning, how many groups of a given size (20 ÷ 5 = 4 bags).
Writing the numbers in the wrong order (3 ÷ 24) — the total being split always comes first.

days.guide: Deal 24 counters one at a time into 3 cups and count one cup: 24 ÷ 3 = 8. Repeat with 4, 6 and 8 cups. The child writes a division equation each time.

questions.q: Share 24 counters among 4 cups. How many in each?
Share 24 among 8 cups.

days.guide: Now the group size is known: put 20 grapes into bags of 5 and count the bags (4). The child records several 'how many groups' problems.

questions.q: 20 grapes go in bags of 5. How many bags?
18 socks are put in pairs. How many pairs?

days.guide: Start at 15 on a number line and jump back by 3s until you reach 0; count the jumps (5). The child shows 4 problems this way.

questions.q: Show 12 ÷ 4 on a number line.
questions.a: Jump back 4s: 12 → 8 → 4 → 0 is 3 jumps, so 12 ÷ 4 = 3.

questions.q: How many jumps of 5 from 30 to 0?

days.guide: For each story ask 'Do we know the number of groups or the size of each group?' The child solves 6 problems and labels each 'sharing' or 'grouping'.

questions.q: 28 cards are shared by 4 friends. How many each? Which kind?
questions.a: 7 each; sharing (number of groups known).

questions.q: 30 kids make teams of 6. How many teams? Which kind?
questions.a: 5 teams; grouping (group size known).

days.guide: Give the quiz; then the child writes one sharing and one grouping problem and solves them. Have the child read their problems to you and label which is sharing and which is grouping.

questions.q: Write a grouping problem for 16 ÷ 2.
questions.a: Example: 16 shoes are put into pairs. How many pairs? 8 pairs.

weeks.assessment_key: 1) 12 ÷ 3 = 4 2) 20 ÷ 4 = 5 3) 18 ÷ 6 = 3 4) 35 ÷ 5 = 7 5) 40 ÷ 10 = 4 6) 24 cookies shared by 6 kids → 4 each (sharing) 7) 21 flowers, 3 per vase → 7 vases (grouping) 8) 16 ÷ 4 on a number line → 4 jumps of 4. Written problems: proficient if both are correctly modeled and solved. Proficient overall: 7+/8.

weeks.prep: Make triangle fact cards (product at the top corner, factors at the bottom corners) for 8 fact families. Write the 20-item quiz in the answer key.
misconceptions: Treating ? ÷ 4 = 7 as 7 ÷ 4 — ask 'What number split into 4 groups gives 7 in each?' and use multiplication (4 × 7 = 28).
Writing fact families with unrelated numbers — every equation in a family uses the same three numbers.

days.guide: Cover a corner of a triangle card (3, 8, 24) and explain the three numbers make 4 facts: 3 × 8 = 24, 8 × 3 = 24, 24 ÷ 3 = 8, 24 ÷ 8 = 3. The child writes families for 8 cards.

questions.q: Write the fact family for 6, 7, 42.
Write the fact family for 5, 9, 45.

days.guide: Model finding a missing factor with a triangle card or by skip counting. The child solves 15 equations, saying the related fact aloud.
Build an array of 35 tiles in 5 rows and count how many are in each row (7). Write 35 ÷ 5 = 7 and 5 × 7 = 35 under it. The child builds 4 more.

questions.q: Use an array to explain 35 ÷ 5.
questions.a: 35 tiles in 5 equal rows gives 7 in each row, so 5 × ? = 35 means ? = 7.

questions.q: What multiplication fact helps solve 48 ÷ 6?

days.guide: Complete puzzle grids where some factors and products are missing. Ask the child to explain how one known fact unlocks another.

questions.q: If you know 9 × 4 = 36, what is 36 ÷ 9?

days.guide: Give the 20-item quiz. Mark errors and have the child write the related multiplication fact for each missed item.

weeks.prep: Tape diagram templates, a ruler and string, bake sale ideas. Write the Unit 2 test in the answer key.
misconceptions: Choosing an operation from one word ('each' means multiply) — decide with a tape diagram whether the total is known or unknown.
Dividing measurement amounts but dropping units (writing 8, not 8 feet) — always label the answer.

days.guide: Draw a tape split into equal sections; label the whole and one section. Show both 'find the total' (multiply) and 'find one section' (divide). The child diagrams and solves 6 problems.

questions.q: 5 boxes hold 8 markers each. How many markers?
questions.a: 40 — a tape of 5 sections of 8.

questions.q: 36 stickers fill 4 pages equally. How many on each page?

days.guide: Act out cutting a length of string into equal pieces. The child draws a line split into equal parts for each measurement problem.

questions.q: A rope 32 feet long is cut into 4 equal pieces. How long is each piece?
questions.a: 8 feet.

questions.q: A ribbon was cut into 6 pieces, each 5 inches long. How long was the ribbon?
questions.a: 30 inches.

days.guide: Put 10 problems on cards; the child sorts them into multiply or divide piles and justifies each choice to you. Ask 'Is the total known or unknown?' whenever the child hesitates.

questions.q: There are 7 tables with 4 chairs each. Multiply or divide? Answer?
questions.a: Multiply — the number of groups and the group size are known, the total is unknown: 28 chairs.

questions.q: 63 cookies go in bags of 9. Multiply or divide? Answer?
questions.a: Divide — the total is known: 7 bags.

days.guide: The child writes and solves a multiplication story and a division story about a bake sale, with a tape diagram for each. Have the child solve each story two ways (drawing and equation) to check.

questions.q: 6 trays hold 5 muffins each. How many muffins?
questions.a: 30 muffins.

questions.q: 24 brownies are packed 4 to a box. How many boxes?
questions.a: 6 boxes.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test without help. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: What two meanings can 18 ÷ 3 have?
questions.a: Sharing: 18 split into 3 groups gives 6 in each. Grouping: 18 split into groups of 3 makes 6 groups.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test: 1) 4 groups of 7 → 4 × 7 = 28 2) Array of 3 rows of 9 → 27 3) If 8 × 6 = 48 then 6 × 8 = 48 4) 30 ÷ 5 = 6 5) 7 × ? = 56 → 8 6) ? ÷ 3 = 9 → 27 7) 45 pencils shared by 9 kids → 5 each 8) 6 bags of 8 rolls → 48 rolls 9) A 40-inch board cut into 5 equal pieces → 8 inches each 10) Fact family for 4, 9, 36 → 4 × 9 = 36, 9 × 4 = 36, 36 ÷ 4 = 9, 36 ÷ 9 = 4. Proficient: 8+/10.

weeks.prep: Hundreds chart, fact cards for 0, 1, 2, 5 and 10, an analog clock and some nickels.
misconceptions: Thinking 8 × 0 = 8 (mixing up with addition) — 8 groups of nothing is nothing; show 8 empty plates.
Confusing × 1 with + 1 (6 × 1 = 7) — one group of 6 is 6.

days.guide: Color multiples of 2 and of 10 on a hundreds chart; notice 2s products are even and 10s end in 0. Connect 2s facts to doubles (2 × 7 = 7 + 7). Practice with cards for 10 minutes.

questions.q: What is 2 × 9? How do doubles help?
What is 10 × 6?

days.guide: Count by 5s around a clock face (each number is 5 minutes) and with nickels. Point out that every 5s product ends in 0 or 5.

questions.q: What is 7 × 5? Use the clock.
questions.a: 35 — the minute hand on the 7 means 35 minutes.

questions.q: How much are 9 nickels worth?
questions.a: 45 cents.

days.guide: Show 0 plates with 5 counters, then 5 plates with 0 counters — both make 0. Show that any number × 1 is itself. The child writes why 8 × 0 = 0 in a sentence.

questions.q: Why does 8 × 0 = 0?
questions.a: 8 groups of 0 is nothing at all, so the product is 0.

questions.q: What is 1 × 47?

days.guide: Build a 10 × 4 array and cover half of it; the half showing is 5 × 4. The child explains in words why 5s products are half of 10s products for 3 facts.

questions.q: If 10 × 8 = 80, what is 5 × 8, and why?
questions.a: 40 — 5 groups is half of 10 groups, and half of 80 is 40.

questions.q: Use the pattern to find 5 × 6.
questions.a: Half of 10 × 6 = 60, so 30.

days.guide: Give an untimed 20-fact check (2s, 5s, 10s, 0s, 1s, with some division). The child records missed facts on a practice card.

questions.q: What is 5 × 9? What is 20 ÷ 2?

weeks.prep: Grid paper, colored pencils, a deck of playing cards (face cards removed; ace = 1) for fact war. Write the quiz in the answer key.
misconceptions: Thinking 3 × 7 is 2 × 7 + 1 (adding 1 instead of one more group of 7) — show the extra row in an array.
Splitting an array but multiplying only one part (6 × 7 = 5 × 7 = 35) — color both parts and add them.

days.guide: Draw a 2 × 6 array, then add one more row: 3 × 6 = 2 × 6 + 6 = 12 + 6 = 18. The child solves all the 3s facts this way and records them.

questions.q: Use 2 × 8 to find 3 × 8.
questions.a: 2 × 8 = 16; add one more 8 to get 24.

questions.q: What is 3 × 7?

days.guide: Show that 4 × 6 is double 2 × 6 (12 + 12 = 24). The child makes a table of 2s facts and doubles each to get the 4s.

questions.q: Find 4 × 7 by doubling.
questions.a: 2 × 7 = 14; double 14 is 28.

questions.q: Find 4 × 9.
questions.a: 36 (double 18).

days.guide: Draw a 6 × 7 array and draw a line after 5 rows; color 5 × 7 = 35 and 1 × 7 = 7, total 42. Name this the distributive property. The child splits 4 arrays.

questions.q: Split 6 × 7 into easier facts.
Split 4 × 8 into two equal parts.

days.guide: Teach 6s as 5s plus one group (6 × 8 = 40 + 8 = 48) or as 3s doubled. Play fact war: each player flips 2 cards and multiplies; the larger product wins.

questions.q: Find 6 × 8 using 5s.
questions.a: 5 × 8 = 40, plus 8 more = 48.

questions.q: Find 6 × 6.

days.guide: Give the mixed quiz; then the child explains one fact with the distributive property in writing, with a split array. Look for a split array drawn and both partial products added.

questions.q: Explain 4 × 9 with the distributive property.

weeks.assessment_key: 3 × 4 = 12, 3 × 6 = 18, 3 × 9 = 27, 4 × 4 = 16, 4 × 6 = 24, 4 × 8 = 32, 6 × 3 = 18, 6 × 7 = 42, 6 × 9 = 54, 6 × 6 = 36, 24 ÷ 4 = 6, 18 ÷ 3 = 6, 42 ÷ 6 = 7, 36 ÷ 4 = 9, 27 ÷ 3 = 9. Proficient: 13+/15. Distributive explanation: 3 = correct split, both parts multiplied and added, with drawing; 2 = correct split with a minor error; 1 = no valid split.

weeks.prep: Multiplication chart (blank and filled), fact cards, a simple path board game and a die. Write the 40 facts (all facts 0–10, mixed) for Friday.
misconceptions: Thinking the associative property changes the numbers — only the grouping changes: (2 × 4) × 3 = 2 × (4 × 3) = 24.
Misusing the 9s finger trick (putting the wrong finger down) — check with 10s minus a group: 9 × 7 = 70 − 7 = 63.

days.guide: List 9 × 1 through 9 × 10 and notice the tens digit is one less than the other factor and the digits add to 9. Teach 9 × n = 10 × n − n and the finger trick. The child practices 10 facts.

questions.q: Find 9 × 7 using tens.
What patterns do the 9s products have?
questions.a: The digits add to 9 (18, 27, 36 …), and the tens digit is one less than the other factor.

days.guide: Double 4s to find 8s (8 × 6 = 24 + 24 = 48). Then solve 2 × 4 × 3 as (2 × 4) × 3 = 8 × 3 and as 2 × (4 × 3) = 2 × 12; both are 24 — the associative property.

questions.q: Find 8 × 7 by doubling.
questions.a: 4 × 7 = 28; double is 56.

questions.q: Solve 2 × 4 × 3 two ways.

days.guide: Split 7 into 5 + 2: 7 × 6 = 5 × 6 + 2 × 6 = 30 + 12 = 42. Play a board game where you answer a 7s fact to move ahead.

questions.q: Find 7 × 8 using 5s and 2s.
What is 7 × 7?

days.guide: Shade the square numbers on the diagonal of a multiplication table and color all even products. Discuss why the table is symmetric (commutative property) and why every product in the 2s, 4s, 6s, 8s and 10s rows is even.

questions.q: Why is every product in the 6s row even?
questions.a: 6 = 2 × 3, so 6 × any number is 2 × something — a double — which is always even.

questions.q: Name the square numbers on the diagonal up to 10 × 10.

days.guide: Give a 40-fact mixed check. The child counts correct facts and sets a goal, such as 'learn my 7s and 8s by next Friday.'

questions.q: What is 8 × 9? What is 56 ÷ 7?

weeks.assessment_key: Key for commonly missed facts: 7 × 8 = 56, 6 × 7 = 42, 8 × 8 = 64, 9 × 6 = 54, 7 × 9 = 63, 8 × 4 = 32, 7 × 4 = 28, 9 × 9 = 81, 8 × 6 = 48, 3 × 7 = 21, 9 × 3 = 27, 6 × 8 = 48, 7 × 7 = 49, 63 ÷ 9 = 7, 72 ÷ 8 = 9, 49 ÷ 7 = 7, 54 ÷ 6 = 9, 64 ÷ 8 = 8, 42 ÷ 7 = 6, 56 ÷ 8 = 7 (check all others against a multiplication chart). Proficient: 36+/40 (90%), with a written goal for missed facts.

weeks.prep: Base-ten rods, fact cards, internet access for a Math Playground division game. Write the Unit 3 test in the answer key.
misconceptions: 'Just add a zero' without understanding — say '4 × 3 tens = 12 tens = 120' so the zero comes from place value.
Losing a zero when the basic fact already ends in 0 (5 × 40 = 20) — 5 × 4 tens = 20 tens = 200.

days.guide: Lay out 4 groups of 3 rods; count 12 rods = 12 tens = 120. Record 4 × 30 = 4 × 3 tens = 12 tens = 120. The child models 6 more.

questions.q: Find 4 × 30.
Find 6 × 50 using tens.
questions.a: 6 × 5 tens = 30 tens = 300.

days.guide: Solve pairs of facts: 6 × 7 = 42 and 6 × 70 = 420. The child explains the pattern: the product is 10 times bigger because one factor is 10 times bigger.

questions.q: Find 6 × 7 and 6 × 70.
Find 9 × 80.

days.guide: Solve 6 word problems and check each by skip counting by tens or using the tens fact. Ask the child to say each problem as 'groups of tens' before solving (8 × 4 tens = 32 tens).

questions.q: 8 boxes have 40 crayons each. How many crayons?
A bus holds 60 people. How many people fit in 3 buses?

days.guide: Practice division facts with fact family cards, then play 10 minutes of an online fact game. Record facts that were slow.

questions.q: What is 81 ÷ 9, and what multiplication fact proves it?

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test plus a 30-fact fluency check of mixed facts. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: What is 7 × 60?

weeks.prep: Square tiles (or 1-inch paper squares), sticky notes, centimeter and inch grid paper, a 12-inch square of paper for a square-foot template, a ruler.
misconceptions: Leaving gaps or overlapping units — units must cover the shape with no gaps or overlaps; show that a messy covering gives a wrong count.
Confusing area with perimeter (counting edges) — area counts the squares inside.

days.guide: Cover a book with sticky notes edge to edge, count them, and say 'The area is 9 sticky notes.' Try a placemat. Discuss why different-sized units give different counts.

questions.q: Why might a book measure 6 sticky notes but 20 smaller squares?
questions.a: The units are different sizes; smaller units need more to cover the same area.

questions.q: What does area measure?
questions.a: How much flat space a shape covers.

days.guide: Count squares inside shapes on centimeter and inch grid paper; write answers in square centimeters or square inches. Model counting row by row so no square is missed or counted twice, and point out half-squares are not used yet.

questions.q: A rectangle on centimeter grid paper covers 3 rows of 5 squares. What is its area?
questions.a: 15 square centimeters.

questions.q: Is a square inch bigger or smaller than a square centimeter?
questions.a: Bigger (an inch is about 2 1/2 centimeters).

days.guide: The child arranges 12 tiles into three different shapes (e.g., 3 × 4, 2 × 6, an L shape). Ask why they all have the same area.

questions.q: Do a 2 × 6 rectangle and a 3 × 4 rectangle have the same area?
questions.a: Yes — both are 12 square units because both use 12 tiles.

questions.q: Can shapes look different but have equal areas?
questions.a: Yes, if they cover the same number of square units.

days.guide: Make a 12 in × 12 in square-foot template. Estimate how many fit on a rug, then measure by laying the template down and marking.

questions.q: A rug is 3 square-foot templates long and 2 wide. What is its area?
questions.a: 6 square feet.

questions.q: Would you measure a room in square inches or square feet?
questions.a: Square feet — square inches are too small.

days.guide: Give 10 grid shapes to measure (see answer key). The child writes why units must not overlap or leave gaps.

questions.q: Why can't area units overlap?
questions.a: Overlapping squares get counted twice and make the area too big; gaps leave space uncounted.

weeks.assessment_key: Draw on grid paper: 1) 2 × 3 rectangle → 6 sq units 2) 4 × 4 → 16 3) 1 × 7 → 7 4) 3 × 5 → 15 5) L shape made of a 3 × 2 and a 1 × 2 → 8 6) 2 × 6 → 12 7) 5 × 2 → 10 8) 3 × 3 → 9 9) T shape: 3 × 1 top plus 1 × 2 stem → 5 10) 4 × 2 → 8. Proficient: 9+/10 and an explanation that mentions both gaps and overlaps.

weeks.prep: Square tiles, ruler, grid paper. Write the 8 area problems in the answer key for Friday.
misconceptions: Adding side lengths instead of multiplying (3 + 5 = 8 for area) — tile the rectangle to show 3 rows of 5 = 15.
Forgetting square units — area is labeled in square units (sq ft), not feet.

days.guide: Tile a 4 × 6 rectangle and count every tile, then point out 4 rows of 6 = 4 × 6 = 24. The child tiles 4 rectangles and writes both methods.

questions.q: A rectangle has 4 rows of 6 tiles. What is its area?
questions.a: 24 square units.

questions.q: Why does multiplying work for area?
questions.a: The tiles form an array: rows × tiles in each row = total tiles.

days.guide: Measure side lengths of grid-paper rectangles with a ruler and multiply. The child finds 8 areas with units.

questions.q: A rectangle is 7 cm by 3 cm. What is its area?
questions.a: 21 square centimeters.

questions.q: A square has 9-inch sides. What is its area?
questions.a: 81 square inches.

days.guide: Use an unknown-factor equation: 4 × ? = 24. Draw the rectangle with one side marked '?'.

questions.q: A rug has area 24 sq ft and width 4 ft. How long is it?
questions.a: 6 feet.

questions.q: A garden has area 45 sq m and length 9 m. What is its width?
questions.a: 5 meters.

days.guide: Draw a 7 × 8 rectangle and split it into 7 × 5 and 7 × 3; find 35 + 21 = 56. Connect this to the distributive property.

questions.q: Find 7 × 8 by splitting the rectangle.
Split 6 × 9 into two rectangles.

days.guide: Give the 8 area problems. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: What is the area of an 8 by 4 rectangle?
questions.a: 32 square units.

weeks.assessment_key: 1) 5 × 6 → 30 sq units 2) 8 cm × 3 cm → 24 sq cm 3) 9 ft × 9 ft → 81 sq ft 4) Area 36, one side 4 → other side 9 5) Area 56, one side 7 → 8 6) 7 × 8 = 7 × 5 + 7 × 3 → 35 + 21 = 56 7) 6 × 7 = 6 × 5 + 6 × 2 → 30 + 12 = 42 8) A 10 m by 4 m patio → 40 sq m. Proficient: 7+/8 with correct units.

weeks.prep: Grid paper, colored pencils. Draw several L- and T-shaped figures with labeled sides. Write the Unit 4 test in the answer key.
misconceptions: Counting a section twice when splitting shapes — color each rectangle differently so no square belongs to two parts.
Missing an unlabeled side on an L shape — find it by subtracting from the opposite side.

days.guide: Draw an L shape and split it with a line into two rectangles; color each, find each area, then add. The child does 5.

questions.q: An L shape splits into a 4 × 3 and a 2 × 2 rectangle. What is its area?
questions.a: 12 + 4 = 16 square units.

questions.q: Why do we add the two areas?
questions.a: The whole shape is made of the two parts with no overlap.

days.guide: Split the same figure horizontally and then vertically, or find a big rectangle and subtract the missing corner. Both answers should match.

questions.q: A 6 × 5 rectangle has a 2 × 2 corner cut out. What is its area?
questions.a: 30 − 4 = 26 square units.

questions.q: If two methods give different answers, what does that mean?
questions.a: One method has an error — a part was missed or counted twice.

days.guide: The child designs a dream bedroom on grid paper (1 square = 1 sq ft) with a bed, desk and rug drawn as rectangles, and labels each area. Remind the child to split any L-shaped space into rectangles before multiplying, and check two of their areas with a calculator.

questions.q: A bed is 4 ft by 7 ft. What is its area?
questions.a: 28 sq ft.

questions.q: The room is 10 ft by 12 ft. What is its area?

days.guide: Solve garden and patio area problems by drawing and splitting. Model the first problem, then let the child do the rest while you check that every part of each shape is counted once.

questions.q: An L-shaped patio is made of a 5 × 4 ft and a 3 × 2 ft rectangle. What is its area?
A garden plot is 8 m by 6 m. What is its area?
questions.a: 48 sq m.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: What units is area measured in?
questions.a: Square units (sq cm, sq in, sq ft, sq m).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test: 1) Shape of 3 rows of 4 squares → 12 sq units 2) 6 × 4 rectangle → 24 3) 9 m × 5 m → 45 sq m 4) Area 42, one side 6 → 7 5) 8 × 7 = 8 × 5 + 8 × 2 → 40 + 16 = 56 6) L shape of 5 × 3 and 2 × 2 → 19 7) 8 × 6 rectangle minus a 2 × 3 corner → 42 8) Why can't units overlap? → overlaps count the same space twice. Proficient: 7+/8.

weeks.prep: Bar model templates; a pretend party price list (plates $4 per pack of 10, cups $3 per pack of 8, $40 to spend). Write the quiz in the answer key.
misconceptions: Stopping after step one — underline the question and check that the final answer answers it.
Using the wrong operation in step two — draw a bar model for each step.

days.guide: Read a two-step problem aloud, underline the question, and write 'Step 1: find …, Step 2: find …' before doing any math. The child plans 5 problems, then solves them.

questions.q: Mia has 3 packs of 8 pencils and gives away 5. How many are left?
questions.a: Step 1: 3 × 8 = 24. Step 2: 24 − 5 = 19 pencils.

questions.q: Tom buys 4 books at $6 each and pays with $30. How much change?

days.guide: Write a single equation with a letter for the unknown, e.g., p = 3 × 8 − 5, doing multiplication or division before adding or subtracting (use parentheses to make it clear). The child writes and solves 5.

questions.q: Write and solve an equation: 5 bags of 6 apples, then 7 apples are eaten.
Solve n = 48 ÷ 6 + 9.

days.guide: Before solving, round and estimate; after solving, compare. The child writes 'reasonable' or 'not reasonable' for each.

questions.q: Estimate, then solve: 198 + 315 − 107.
questions.a: Estimate 200 + 300 − 100 = 400; exact 406 — reasonable.

questions.q: Lee says 7 × 9 − 20 = 83. Is that reasonable?

days.guide: Pose the party problem: 24 guests, plates in packs of 10 for $4, cups in packs of 8 for $3, and $40 to spend. The child finds the packs needed, the cost and the change.

questions.q: How many packs of 10 plates are needed for 24 guests, and what do they cost?
questions.a: 3 packs (2 packs is only 20 plates) — $12.

questions.q: How many packs of 8 cups for 24 guests, what do they cost, and how much change is left from $40 after plates and cups?

days.guide: Give the quiz and have the child explain one solution with a bar model. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Jen reads 15 pages a day for 4 days, then 12 more pages. How many pages in all?

weeks.assessment_key: 1) 6 boxes of 8 crayons, 9 lost → 39 2) $50 minus 3 games at $9 each → $23 3) 36 kids in 4 equal teams, then 2 more kids join each team → 11 per team 4) 125 + 248 − 90 → 283 5) 7 rows of 6 chairs, 12 empty → 30 filled 6) 45 ÷ 5 + 18 → 27. Proficient: 5+/6 and a bar-model explanation with both steps labeled.

weeks.prep: Addition table (0–10) and multiplication table (0–10), colored pencils. Write the Unit 5 test and a 20-fact mixed check.
misconceptions: Believing odd × odd is even — test examples: 3 × 5 = 15 is odd.
Naming an input/output rule from only one pair — check the rule against every row.

days.guide: The child tests many examples and fills a chart for even + even, even + odd, odd + odd, then the same for products, and states the rules. Ask the child to explain why the rule works using pairs (an odd number always has one left over).

questions.q: Is odd + odd even or odd? Give an example.
Is even × odd even or odd?

days.guide: Color patterns in the addition table (equal sums along diagonals, rows increasing by 1). The child writes 3 rules.

questions.q: What happens moving down one column of the addition table?
questions.a: Each sum increases by 1.

questions.q: Along a diagonal from bottom-left to top-right, what stays the same?
questions.a: The sums are all equal (3 + 5, 4 + 4, 5 + 3 all equal 8).

days.guide: Fill in input/output tables and name each rule (× 4, + 7, ÷ 5 …). Check the rule on every pair.

questions.q: In: 2, 3, 5 → Out: 8, 12, 20. What is the rule, and what is the output for 7?
In: 10, 15, 20 → Out: 2, 3, 4. What is the rule?

days.guide: The child writes why 4 times any number is even: 4 × n = 2 × (2 × n), so it is a double, and doubles are always even. Ask them to test the rule with three numbers, including an odd one, before writing.

questions.q: Why is 4 × 7 even?
questions.a: 4 × 7 = 2 × 14 — a double — and doubles are even, so 28 is even.

questions.q: Is 4 × 9 even?
questions.a: Yes, 36.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test plus the 20-fact mixed check. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Is odd × odd even or odd?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test: 1) 4 packs of 6 juice boxes, 5 drunk → 19 2) $40 − 3 × $8 → $16 3) Equation with a letter for #2 → m = 40 − 3 × 8 4) 7 + 9 even or odd → even 5) 5 × 7 even or odd → odd 6) In 1, 2, 3 → Out 6, 12, 18: rule × 6, output for 5 = 30 7) Why is 2 × any number even? → it is a double. Proficient: 6+/7 and 18+/20 facts.

weeks.prep: Paper rectangles, circles and squares; scissors; 12-inch paper strips (6 per child) for fraction strips; markers; an envelope to store strips.
misconceptions: Calling unequal parts 'fourths' — fractions need equal parts; cut and stack the parts to compare.
Thinking a larger denominator means a bigger piece — 1/8 is smaller than 1/4 because the whole is cut into more parts.

days.guide: Fold rectangles and circles into halves, thirds (fold into a Z), fourths, sixths and eighths. Count the parts and name them.

questions.q: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. What is one slice called?
questions.a: One sixth (1/6).

questions.q: How many fourths make a whole?

days.guide: Label each part with a unit fraction 1/b. Show a circle cut into 4 unequal parts and ask if each part is 1/4.

questions.q: Is a shape cut into 3 unequal pieces showing thirds?
questions.a: No — thirds must be 3 equal parts.

questions.q: What does the 8 in 1/8 tell you?
questions.a: The whole is cut into 8 equal parts.

days.guide: Partition paper squares into fourths three ways (4 strips, 4 small squares, 4 triangles using both diagonals). Cut and overlay to prove each part has equal area.

questions.q: Can triangle-shaped fourths and strip-shaped fourths of the same square be equal?
questions.a: Yes — each is 1/4 of the same square, so each has the same area even though the shapes differ.

questions.q: A square made of 16 small squares is split into 4 equal parts. How many small squares are in each part?

days.guide: Make strips all the same length: whole, halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, eighths; label every piece. Save them in an envelope for the unit.

questions.q: Which is longer, 1/3 or 1/6?
How many eighths fit on one half?

days.guide: Give the 10-item identification check. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Draw a rectangle and shade 1/5.
questions.a: A rectangle split into 5 equal parts with 1 part shaded.

weeks.assessment_key: 1) Circle in 2 equal parts, 1 shaded → 1/2 2) Rectangle in 4, 1 shaded → 1/4 3) Hexagon in 6 → 1/6 4) Bar in 8 → 1/8 5) Triangle in 3 equal parts → 1/3 6) Square in 4 unequal parts → 'not fourths — the parts aren't equal' 7–10) Draw 1/2, 1/3, 1/6, 1/8 with equal parts. Proficient: 9+/10.

weeks.prep: Fraction strips from last week, pattern blocks (or printed paper ones), 8 counters in two colors.
misconceptions: Reading 3/4 as '3 and 4' — say '3 fourths,' meaning 3 pieces of size 1/4.
Writing the unshaded count as the numerator — the numerator counts the parts being described (shaded).

days.guide: Join three 1/4 strips and say '1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 is 3 fourths, 3/4.' Build 5/6 and 2/3 the same way.

questions.q: How many 1/6 pieces make 5/6?
What is 2/3 made of?
questions.a: Two 1/3 pieces.

days.guide: Use the yellow hexagon as 1 whole: trapezoid = 1/2, blue rhombus = 1/3, triangle = 1/6. Build fractions like 2/3 (2 rhombuses).

questions.q: How many triangles cover the hexagon, and what fraction is one triangle?
What fraction of the hexagon do 2 rhombuses cover?

days.guide: Line up 8 counters with 3 red: 3/8 are red. Change colors to show other fractions of the set.

questions.q: 8 counters, 3 red. What fraction are red? Not red?
questions.a: 3/8 red; 5/8 not red.

questions.q: 4 of 8 counters are blue. What fraction is blue?
questions.a: 4/8 (also equal to 1/2).

days.guide: Draw pizzas and chocolate bars to solve fraction stories. Ask the child to say what the whole is and how many equal parts it has before writing each fraction.

questions.q: Ana ate 3 of 8 equal slices. What fraction did she eat? What fraction is left?
questions.a: 3/8 eaten; 5/8 left.

questions.q: A bar has 6 equal parts and Ben ate 4. What fraction did he eat?

days.guide: Give 12 shaded models to name and 4 fractions to draw. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Draw 2/5.
questions.a: A whole split into 5 equal parts with 2 shaded.

weeks.prep: Number line strips (0 to 1 and 0 to 2), a ruler marked in halves and fourths of an inch.
misconceptions: Counting tick marks instead of spaces (calling the first mark 1/5 on a line split into 4) — count the jumps (intervals), not the lines.
Starting at 1 instead of 0 — every fraction is a distance from 0.

days.guide: Fold a 0-to-1 strip into 4 equal parts, then mark and label 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4. Repeat for thirds, sixths and eighths.

questions.q: A 0–1 line is split into 3 equal spaces. Label the marks.
How many spaces are needed to show eighths from 0 to 1?

days.guide: Locate 3/4 by counting 3 jumps of 1/4 from 0. Then locate 5/8 and 2/3.

questions.q: How do you find 5/8 on a number line?
questions.a: Split 0 to 1 into 8 equal spaces and count 5 spaces from 0.

questions.q: Is 2/3 closer to 0 or to 1?
questions.a: Closer to 1.

days.guide: Extend lines to 2 and keep counting fourths past 1 (5/4, 6/4, 7/4, 8/4 = 2). Do the same with thirds: 6/3 = 2.

questions.q: Where is 5/4?
questions.a: One fourth past 1.

questions.q: What whole number equals 6/3?

days.guide: Look at a ruler: each inch is a 0-to-1 number line split into halves and fourths. Find 1/2 in, 1 1/4 in and 2 3/4 in.

questions.q: On a ruler, what is halfway between 0 and 1 inch?
questions.a: 1/2 inch.

questions.q: How many fourths of an inch are in 1 inch?

days.guide: Give 10 fractions to place; the child explains how they located two of them. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Explain how you placed 3/6.
questions.a: I split 0 to 1 into 6 equal spaces and counted 3 from 0 — it lands halfway.

weeks.assessment_key: Place: 1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/3, 2/3, 5/6, 3/8, 7/8, 4/4 (at 1), 6/4 (halfway between 1 and 2). Each must be on a line divided into the correct number of equal spaces, counted from 0. Proficient: 9+/10 plus a clear explanation of two placements.

weeks.prep: Fraction strips and stacked number lines (halves, fourths, eighths, all the same length). Make matching cards: 1/2 & 2/4, 1/2 & 4/8, 1/3 & 2/6, 3/4 & 6/8, 1 & 4/4, 2 & 4/2, 3 & 3/1.
misconceptions: Thinking 2/4 is bigger than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger — lay the strips side by side to show they cover the same length.
Thinking whole numbers can't be fractions — 4/4 = 1 and 3/1 = 3.

days.guide: Lay down the 1/2 strip and find other strips that exactly match its length (2/4, 3/6, 4/8). Do the same for 1/3 and 3/4.

questions.q: Name 3 fractions equal to 1/2.
What fraction in sixths equals 1/3?

days.guide: Stack 0–1 lines for halves, fourths and eighths so the 0s and 1s line up. Draw vertical lines through points that match.

questions.q: Which fourths and eighths line up with 1/2?
How many eighths equal 3/4?

days.guide: Show 3 wholes, each as one piece: 3 = 3/1. Show one whole cut into 4: 4/4 = 1; cut into 6: 6/6 = 1.

questions.q: Write 1 as a fraction with denominator 6.
Write 4 as a fraction.

days.guide: Play memory with the equivalent fraction cards; for each match the child proves it with strips or a number line. Make cards for 1/2, 2/4, 4/8, 1/3, 2/6, 3/4, 6/8, 1, 4/4, 2 and 4/2 before starting.

questions.q: Is 2/3 equivalent to 4/6? Explain.
questions.a: Yes — 4 sixths cover the same length as 2 thirds.

questions.q: Is 3/4 equivalent to 3/8?
questions.a: No — eighths are smaller, so 3/8 is less than 3/4.

days.guide: Give the 10-item quiz with strips available for drawing. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

weeks.prep: Fraction strips, paper fraction circles, index cards with fractions for fraction war (use denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, 8).
misconceptions: Thinking 1/6 > 1/3 because 6 > 3 — with the same numerator, a bigger denominator means smaller pieces.
Comparing fractions of different-size wholes — half of a large pizza can be more than half of a small one, so compare only with the same whole.

days.guide: Compare 3/8 and 5/8 with strips: the pieces are the same size, so more pieces is more. Record with <, >, =.

questions.q: Compare 3/8 and 5/8.
questions.a: 3/8 < 5/8 — same-size pieces, and 5 pieces is more.

questions.q: Compare 4/6 and 2/6.

days.guide: Compare 2/3 and 2/6: the same number of pieces, but thirds are bigger. Show with circles.

questions.q: Compare 2/3 and 2/6.
questions.a: 2/3 > 2/6 — thirds are bigger pieces than sixths.

questions.q: Compare 1/8 and 1/4.

days.guide: Draw a big pizza and a small pizza; shade 1/2 of the small one and 1/4 of the big one. Ask which is more pizza — it can be the 1/4! Conclude that comparisons only work with same-size wholes.

questions.q: Is 1/2 always more than 1/4?
questions.a: Only when the wholes are the same size.

questions.q: Why must we compare fractions of the same whole?
questions.a: Because the size of each piece depends on the size of the whole.

days.guide: Play fraction war: each flips a card; compare only pairs with the same numerator or same denominator (flip again otherwise). The child draws to justify each win.

questions.q: Compare 3/4 and 3/6.
questions.a: 3/4 > 3/6 — fourths are bigger than sixths.

questions.q: Compare 5/6 and 6/6.
questions.a: 5/6 < 6/6 (6/6 is one whole).

days.guide: Give 12 comparisons; the child justifies 3 in writing. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Justify 2/4 < 2/3.
questions.a: Same numerator; thirds are bigger pieces than fourths, so 2 thirds is more than 2 fourths.

weeks.prep: Measuring cups (1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 cup), a simple recipe card (e.g., pancakes), a garden rectangle drawing, 3 stations set up (number line, comparing, equivalence). Write 5 worked problems with errors for Thursday and the Unit 6 test.
misconceptions: Thinking a 1/4 cup holds more than a 1/3 cup — fill each and pour into a 1-cup measure to compare.
In error analysis, accepting a larger denominator as a larger fraction — recheck with strips.

days.guide: Read the recipe and measure 1/2, 3/4 and 1/3 cup amounts with water or flour. Ask how many 1/4 cups make 3/4 cup.

questions.q: How many 1/4 cups make 3/4 cup?
How many 1/2 cups make 1 cup?

days.guide: Draw a garden rectangle and split it into 4 or 6 equal plots; label each as a unit fraction of the whole garden. Ask the child to prove the plots are equal by counting squares or measuring.

questions.q: A garden is split into 6 equal plots and 2 are tomatoes. What fraction is tomatoes?
questions.a: 2/6 (equal to 1/3).

questions.q: Each of 4 equal beds is what fraction of the garden?

days.guide: Rotate through the three stations, about 12 minutes each; check work together at the end. Circulate between stations and ask the child to explain one answer at each.

questions.q: Place 3/4 and 1/2 on a 0–1 line. Which is farther right?

days.guide: Show 5 worked problems with mistakes (e.g., '1/6 > 1/3', '3/4 is between 1 and 2', '2/4 is not equal to 1/2'). The child finds and fixes each.

questions.a: 1/6 < 1/3 — sixths are smaller pieces.

questions.q: Fix: 2/4 is not equal to 1/2.
questions.a: 2/4 = 1/2 — they cover the same length on a strip.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: Which is greater, 2/8 or 2/4?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test: 1) 1 of 3 equal parts shaded → 1/3 2) 5 of 8 → 5/8 3) Place 2/4 on a 0–1 number line → halfway 4) 6/6 = 1 5) 4/2 = 2 6) 1/2 = 3/6 7) 2/3 = 4/6 8) 3/8 < 5/8 9) 2/3 > 2/6 10) Why can 1/4 of a big pizza be more than 1/2 of a small pizza? → the wholes are different sizes. Proficient: 8+/10.

weeks.prep: Analog clock with movable hands (or a paper-plate clock), open number line paper. Write the time quiz in the answer key.
misconceptions: Reading the hour hand wrong near the next hour (saying 3:55 is 4:55) — the hour hand points to the hour it has most recently passed.
Treating an hour like 100 minutes (2:50 to 3:10 = 60 minutes) — jump to the next hour on a number line: 10 + 10 = 20 minutes.

days.guide: Count by 5s around the clock then add ones (7:23 is 4 fives + 3 past 7). The child reads and sets 15 times.

questions.q: The hour hand is just past 4; the minute hand is 2 marks past the 7. What time is it?
Show 9:52. Where is the hour hand?
questions.a: Almost at the 10 (between 9 and 10).

days.guide: Use an open number line: 2:45 → 3:00 is 15 min, 3:00 → 3:20 is 20 min; total 35 min. The child solves 8 problems.

questions.q: How long from 2:45 to 3:20?
questions.a: 35 minutes.

questions.q: How long from 10:15 to 11:05?
questions.a: 50 minutes.

days.guide: For an unknown end time, jump forward; for an unknown start time, jump backward. Model one of each on the number line, then the child solves 6 problems, checking each by counting forward from the start time.

questions.q: Practice started at 4:20 and lasted 45 minutes. When did it end?
A show ended at 7:10 after 50 minutes. When did it start?

days.guide: The child records the start and end times of 5 activities in their day and finds the length of each. Have the child draw a number line for any activity that crosses the hour.

questions.q: Lunch was 12:05 to 12:40. How long?
questions.a: 35 minutes.

questions.q: Reading was 1:50 to 2:25. How long?
questions.a: 35 minutes.

days.guide: Give the time quiz. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: How many minutes are in an hour?

weeks.assessment_key: 1) Read a clock showing 3:47 2) Read 11:08 3) Draw hands for 6:34 (hour hand a bit past halfway between 6 and 7) 4) 8:15 to 8:50 → 35 min 5) 1:40 to 2:15 → 35 min 6) Start 9:25, lasts 40 min → ends 10:05 7) Ends 4:00 after 25 min → started 3:35 8) 10:50 to 11:30 → 40 min. Proficient: 7+/8.

weeks.prep: A 1-liter bottle, measuring cups, 5 household containers (mug, pot, vase …), water, a towel. Sketch beaker diagrams with scales counting by 1, 2 and 5 liters.
misconceptions: Thinking taller containers always hold more — pour between a tall thin container and a short wide one.
Misreading scales (counting each mark as 1 L when marks are 2 L apart) — find what each space is worth first.

days.guide: Fill a 1-liter bottle. Show household containers and ask 'More or less than 1 liter?', then test by pouring.

questions.q: Does a bathtub hold more or less than 1 liter?
questions.a: Much more.

questions.q: Does a teacup hold more or less than 1 liter?
questions.a: Less.

days.guide: Use the liter bottle (marked at 1/2 and 1/4 if possible) to measure 5 containers; record results in a table. Have the child estimate before each measurement and record both numbers in the table.

questions.q: A pot holds 3 full liter bottles of water. What is its capacity?
questions.a: 3 liters.

questions.q: A vase holds about half a bottle. About how much is that?
questions.a: About 1/2 liter.

days.guide: Read beaker diagrams: find the scale first, then read the level. Model one diagram aloud ('the marks go up by 2, so this line is 6'), then the child reads 6 more.

questions.q: Marks go 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 L and the water is at the second mark above 0. How much water?
Marks go by 5 L and the water is halfway between 10 and 15. About how much?
questions.a: About 12 1/2 L.

days.guide: Solve liquid-volume word problems by drawing. Have the child draw jugs or bars for each problem and write an equation with units (L).

questions.q: 4 jugs hold 3 L each. How much in all?
A 20 L tank has 7 L used. How much is left?

days.guide: Give the quiz and an estimation challenge: the child guesses each container's capacity, then measures. Read directions aloud if needed but give no hints. Afterward, score it with the answer key and have the child correct each missed item, explaining the fix to you.

questions.q: A 9 L bucket is filled 3 L per trip. How many trips?

weeks.assessment_key: 1) Spoon: more or less than 1 L → less; kitchen sink → more 2) Read a scale (marks by 2) showing 6 L → 6 L 3) 5 bottles × 2 L → 10 L 4) 18 L shared into 3 jugs → 6 L each 5) 15 L + 8 L → 23 L 6) 40 L − 26 L → 14 L. Proficient: 5+/6; estimation is proficient if the child uses the 1-liter benchmark and estimates are reasonable.

weeks.prep: Kitchen scale (grams), paper clips, a 1 kg bag of rice or flour, a coat hanger with string and two paper cups for a balance. Write the Unit 7 test in the answer key.
misconceptions: Thinking bigger objects always have more mass — compare a large balloon with a small rock.
Mixing up grams and kilograms — a paper clip is about 1 gram; a 1 kg bag of rice is 1,000 grams.

days.guide: Hold a paper clip (about 1 g) and the 1 kg bag. Estimate 8 objects and say whether each is better measured in grams or kilograms.

questions.q: Would you measure a pencil in grams or kilograms?
questions.a: Grams.

questions.q: Would you measure a dog in grams or kilograms?
questions.a: Kilograms.

days.guide: Weigh 8 objects on the kitchen scale and compare with the estimates. Have the child record estimate and actual mass side by side and circle the closest estimate.

questions.q: How many grams are in 1 kilogram?
An apple is about 200 g. Is that more or less than 1 kg?
questions.a: Less.

days.guide: Build a hanger balance with a cup on each end and compare two objects; the lower side is heavier. Ask the child to predict which side will go down before placing each pair.

questions.q: Which side of a balance goes down?
questions.a: The side with more mass.

questions.q: If the balance is level, what do you know?
questions.a: The two masses are equal.

days.guide: Solve one-step mass word problems. Have the child draw a simple picture and write an equation with units for each problem.

questions.q: 3 bags of apples have a mass of 4 kg each. What is the total mass?
questions.a: 12 kg.

questions.q: A box has a mass of 45 kg. 18 kg is removed. What is its mass now?
questions.a: 27 kg.
